## Definition
`geo_code` is the resolved geography crosswalk code for a household's survey
area, matched from the raw survey area/region text against
`PARAM-GEO-GMD-CROSSWALK` for the survey's ISO3 code and survey ID year. It
takes the form `<ISO3>_<geo_year>_<geo_source><geo_level>_<geo_id>`, e.g.
`ALB_2021_NUTS3_AL031`. Only the first three segments (ISO3, geo_year,
`geo_source`+`geo_level`) have fixed shape; `geo_id` is the remainder of the
string and may itself contain further underscores or dots (e.g. GADM's
composite codes such as `COD_2022_GADM1_COD.10_1`, where `geo_id` is
`COD.10_1`). Verified against every committed `PARAM-GEO-GMD-CROSSWALK`
record (144 countries, 2,195 unique non-empty values): 0 values deviate from
this form once `geo_id` is treated as the full remainder rather than a
single token.

## Conceptual intent
`geo_code` is the result of matching the survey's representative-level geography
(`subnatidsurvey`) against the stable country geography crosswalk. It is a
separate variable from the survey-derived identifiers: `subnatid1`-`subnatid4`
and `subnatidsurvey` are built directly from the survey data and do NOT depend
on this match. `geo_code` records the single matched crosswalk code once, and
that resolved match is reused by the GAUL codes (`gaul_adm1_code`,
`gaul_adm2_code`) and the prior-boundary identifiers (`subnatid1_prev`-
`subnatid4_prev`).

## Construction notes
Resolve `geo_code` from the survey's representative level (`subnatidsurvey`) —
the `subnatid{N}` level the survey is representative on. Match that
representative-level survey value against `PARAM-GEO-GMD-CROSSWALK` resolved
from the country layer for the survey's ISO3 code and survey ID year.
`survey_labels` holds one or more pipe-separated (`|`) label variants for the
same geography identity (accented/unaccented, cased, punctuation variants) —
normalize both the survey value and the stored variants (case-fold, trim,
collapse whitespace) before comparing.
On a match:
  geo_code = gmd_subnatidsurvey for the matched country_entry_id
Document the matched `country_entry_id` in the do-file notes.
`geo_code` does NOT supply `subnatid1`-`subnatid4`: those are built directly
from the survey data (the "code - label" string) and never from this crosswalk
match. The resolved match is instead reused downstream by `gaul_adm1_code`/
`gaul_adm2_code` (the GAUL `geo_id` when `geo_source=GAUL`) and by the
prior-boundary `subnatid*_prev` variables (via the prior effective-dated
crosswalk period).

## Consistency checks
- `geo_code` must match `<ISO3>_<geo_year>_<geo_source><geo_level>_<geo_id>`,
  where only the first three segments are fixed-shape (3-letter ISO3, 4-digit
  year, source+level token); `geo_id` is everything remaining and may itself
  contain `_` or `.` (e.g. GADM composite codes). Do not parse `geo_code` by
  splitting on every underscore.
- Every non-missing `geo_code` must correspond to exactly one
  `country_entry_id` in the country's `PARAM-GEO-GMD-CROSSWALK`.
- Cross-check that the matched row's `geo_year` is consistent with the
  survey ID year (flag large mismatches for review).
- Some crosswalk rows are legitimately unpopulated placeholders (blank
  `geo_source`, `geo_level`, and all `gmd_subnatid*`/`gmd_subnatidsurvey`
  fields) — these must resolve to `.c`, not an empty-string `geo_code`.

## Escalation triggers
- No `PARAM-GEO-GMD-CROSSWALK` record is valid for the survey's ISO3 code and
  survey ID year. Apply the registry's `block_and_escalate` fallback policy.
- The survey area text does not match any `survey_labels` entry for the
  resolved country/year. Do not guestimate a geography code from a partial
  or fuzzy match beyond normalized exact matching.
- The survey area text matches more than one `country_entry_id` ambiguously
  (e.g. duplicate `survey_labels` across rows after normalization).

## Common mistakes
- Matching against raw, non-normalized survey label text (case/accent/
  whitespace differences causing false misses).
- Treating `geo_code` as the source of `subnatid1`-`subnatid4`: those are
  survey-derived ("code - label") and independent of this crosswalk match.
- Using a crosswalk record from the wrong ISO3 code or survey ID year.
- Splitting `geo_code` into segments on every underscore — `geo_id` (the
  final segment) can itself contain underscores or dots and must be treated
  as the remainder after the third underscore, not re-split further.
- Treating a blank/placeholder crosswalk row (no `geo_source`/`geo_level`
  populated) as a match instead of escalating.

## Definition
`subnatid1` is the country-specific categorical variable that identifies the
highest-level administrative subdivision within a country's administrative
structure, typically a province or state. Each household is assigned to the
first-level administrative division in which it is located.

## Conceptual intent
`subnatid1` provides the first-level subnational geographic context for every
household and underpins regional disaggregation across the GMD. Along with the
related subnational identifiers it supports analysis of regional inequities and
the construction of subnational statistics that are uniquely identifiable in a
global context.

## Construction notes
`subnatid1` is a string variable that holds country-specific categorical values
as they appear in the source survey. The value is constructed from the actual
survey data, not from the GMD geo crosswalk: it is a single text token made from
the survey's encoded code and the corresponding area label, for example
"6 - Gjirokaster", "6 – Gjirokaster", "6-GJIROKASTER", or "6-Gjirokaster".
The numeric part comes from the survey's own code for the first administrative
level; the text part comes from the label or area name recorded in the raw data.
The number can differ across surveys or years, and spelling/variant differences
must be preserved as they occur in the source data rather than normalized to a
single canonical case. The construction is therefore data-driven and survey-
anchored, with no requirement to retrieve a GMD crosswalk record for the value.
Because the value space is country-specific, `value_codes` is intentionally
left null and must not be fabricated. The agent should build the string from the
observed survey code and label combination and record any variant spelling or
punctuation differences in the do-file notes.

## Consistency checks
- `subnatid1` must be a string variable, not a numeric categorical; verify no
  numeric placeholder codes remain unformatted.
- No household may carry a standard missing (`.`) for `subnatid1`; every case
  must receive a valid country code or an explicit extended missing code.
- Cross-check against `subnatid2`: every second-level division must map to
  exactly one first-level division.
- Verify the codes used match the most recent administrative classification
  pertaining to that survey and that the mapping to the official shapefile is
  consistent.

## Escalation triggers
- The survey's first-level administrative classification cannot be located or
  matched to any official administrative codebook or shapefile.
- A household cannot be assigned to any first-level division.
- The country administrative boundaries changed during the survey ID year and
  the correct classification cannot be determined.

## Common mistakes
- Leaving `subnatid1` as a numeric categorical instead of a string variable.
- Fabricating value codes instead of using the country-specific administrative
  classification.
- Mixing administrative levels (e.g., assigning a second-level code to a
  household) within the same variable.
- Recoding numeric entries without the "code - name" string convention.

## Definition
`subnatid2` is the country-specific categorical variable that identifies the
second-highest level within a country's administrative structure, typically a
district. Each household is assigned to the second-level administrative
division in which it is located.

## Conceptual intent
`subnatid2` locates households at the second administrative level, enabling
finer regional disaggregation than `subnatid1`. It supports subnational
statistics and policy analysis at a more localized geographic granularity.

## Construction notes
`subnatid2` is a string variable with country-specific categorical values as
they appear in the source survey. The value is constructed from the actual
survey data, not from the GMD geo crosswalk: it is a single text token made from
the survey's encoded code and the corresponding area label, for example
"6 - Gjirokaster", "6 – Gjirokaster", "6-GJIROKASTER", or "6-Gjirokaster".
The numeric part comes from the survey's own code for the second administrative
level; the text part comes from the label or area name recorded in the raw data.
The number can differ across surveys or years, and spelling/variant differences
must be preserved as they occur in the source data rather than normalized to a
single canonical case. The construction is therefore data-driven and survey-
anchored, with no requirement to retrieve a GMD crosswalk record for the value.
Households for which the survey only records the first administrative level
may have `subnatid2` missing; use an explicit missing code and document the
reason.

## Consistency checks
- `subnatid2` must be a string variable. Verify no unformatted numeric
  placeholder codes remain.
- Every second-level division must nest under exactly one first-level division
  (`subnatid1`).
- No household may carry a standard missing (`.`) without an explicit extended
  missing code when the level was collected.
- Verify codes match the most recent administrative classification pertaining to
  that survey.

## Escalation triggers
- The survey's second-level administrative classification cannot be matched to
  an official codebook or shapefile.
- A first-level division contains second-level codes that are inconsistent with
  the official nesting.
- The country administrative boundaries changed during the survey ID year and
  the correct classification cannot be determined.

## Common mistakes
- Leaving `subnatid2` numeric instead of string.
- Fabricating value codes instead of using the country administrative
  classification.
- Assigning second-level codes that do not nest within the recorded
  `subnatid1`.
- Recoding numeric entries without the "code - name" string convention.

## Definition
`subnatidsurvey` is a country-specific, string variable that records the lowest
administrative level at which the survey is representative, restricted to the
level that is actually present in the survey's own `subnatid1` through
`subnatid4` hierarchy. It must be a direct value drawn from one of those
variables, not an independent geography code or label invented outside the
survey-admin structure.

## Conceptual intent
`subnatidsurvey` documents the effective level of subnational representativeness
of the survey, but only for the geography that is genuinely mappable within the
survey's own administrative hierarchy. It tells analysts the deepest level of
coverage actually supported by the survey's admin variables without drifting to
an external geo layer or an unsupported raw label.

## Construction notes
`subnatidsurvey` is a string variable with country-specific values and must be
constructed only from the survey's coded administrative geography already
represented in `subnatid1`, `subnatid2`, `subnatid3`, or `subnatid4`. In other
words, the value should be the same kind of code-label string already used in
those variables, such as "6 - Gjirokaster", "6 – Gjirokaster",
"6-GJIROKASTER", or "6-Gjirokaster".
The value is not an externally matched GMD crosswalk code and not an arbitrary
raw survey label. It must be exactly the string value from one of the survey's
admin variables corresponding to the lowest representative level in the current
survey design. Across surveys and years, the numeric code may change and the
spelling/variant may differ, but it remains the same value family as the
survey's own `subnatid` hierarchy.
`value_codes` is intentionally null because values derive from the country
survey design and cannot be enumerated in advance.

## Consistency checks
- `subnatidsurvey` must be a string variable.
- The recorded value must be the same code-label family as exactly one of
  `subnatid1`, `subnatid2`, `subnatid3`, or `subnatid4`.
- The level recorded must be consistent with the survey's documented sampling
  design and with the lowest representative level actually present in the
  survey's administrative hierarchy.
- Verify the recorded value matches the survey year/round and is not carried
  over from another round.

## Escalation triggers
- The survey documentation does not state the level at which the survey is
  representative.
- The recorded representative level conflicts with the level implied by the
  completeness pattern of `subnatid1` through `subnatid4`.

## Common mistakes
- Recording a finer level than the survey is actually representative at.
- Confusing `subnatidsurvey` with the presence or absence of a particular
  subnational identifier variable.
- Fabricating a value instead of reading it from the sampling design.

## Definition
`urban` is a binary dummy variable that records whether the household resides
in an urban or rural locality according to the survey's sampling frame. It
takes the value 1 for urban and 0 for rural.

## Conceptual intent
`urban` is the standard residence classification used across the GMD for
rural-urban disaggregation of welfare, poverty, and demographic indicators. It
must follow the national statistics office definition recorded in the source
survey documentation.

## Construction notes
Map the survey's reported locality type directly to the GMD binary code using
the urban/rural definition stated in the survey's sampling documentation. When
the survey provides multiple locality classes, classify them into urban and
rural according to the national definition; document the grouping in the
do-file notes.

## Consistency checks
- No household should have a standard missing value (`.`) for `urban`; every
  case must be either 1 or 0 or carry an explicit extended missing code.
- Cross-check the urban share against the survey's sampling design; large
  departures from the published sampling rate may signal a coding error.
- Verify the `module_id` matches the directory the artifact lives under
  (`geo/` implies `MOD-GEO`).

## Escalation triggers
- The survey documentation does not state how localities were classified, so
  urban/rural cannot be determined reliably.
- The reported urban share differs sharply from the national statistics office
  publication with no sampling explanation.

## Common mistakes
- Using the statistical office's broad regional variable instead of the actual
  locality-type variable for `urban`.
- Coding a missing locality as rural (0) instead of an explicit missing code.
- Ignoring the survey's definition when it differs from the assumed national
  one.

## Definition
`subnatid1_prev` is a country-specific categorical string variable that is coded
as missing unless the classification used for `subnatid1` has changed since the
previous survey. When the classification has changed, it records the `subnatid1`
code used in the previous survey, providing a way to track administrative
splits.

## Conceptual intent
`subnatid1_prev` maintains temporal consistency in subnational identifiers. It
lets analysts construct current administrative units that are "backwards
compatible" with previous surveys, allowing historical comparisons when
province boundaries have changed.

## Construction notes
`subnatid1_prev` is coded as missing for surveys where the first-level
classification has not changed since the previous survey. Where a change occurred
(e.g., a province split), the previous survey's code is recorded so that both
new units carry the previous code. Example: if province "32 - West Java" split
into "32 - West Java" and "36 - Banten", `subnatid1_prev` would contain
"32 - West Java" for both provinces 32 and 36.
**Reusing the geography crosswalk.** Resolve `PARAM-GEO-GMD-CROSSWALK` from
the country layer for the survey's ISO3 code. If the country has more than
one effective-dated record (multiple `effective_from`/`effective_to`
periods), a documented boundary change exists: match the household's area
against the period containing the survey ID year to obtain `subnatid1`, then
match the same geography against the immediately prior period (the record
whose `effective_to` precedes the current period's `effective_from`) to
obtain `subnatid1_prev` from that record's `gmd_subnatid1`. If the country's
crosswalk has only one effective-dated record (no documented boundary
change), `subnatid1_prev` remains coded as missing.
`value_codes` is intentionally null because the previous values depend on the
country's administrative history and the country parameter layer. Load the
country parameters and exceptions valid for the survey's ID year and the
relevant previous survey. Values follow the same "code - name" string convention
as `subnatid1`.

## Consistency checks
- `subnatid1_prev` must be a string variable.
- When populated, its value must be a valid first-level code from the previous

### 3.1 Recode semantics (fixed, evaluated per row)

Order is total and unambiguous — the first matching rule wins:

1. **gate** — if `gate` is set and its `predicate` is **false** for the row →
   assign `gate.else_code`. Gate wins over everything, including a null
   `raw_value` (e.g. a below-`mineducatage` person is `.c` even if education is
   missing).
2. **null** — else if `raw_value` is NaN → `missing_map.null` (required if any
   null can occur; a null with no rule is a hard error, never a silent drop).
3. **value_map** — else if `raw_value` ∈ `value_map` → its canonical code.
4. **specific missing** — else if `raw_value` ∈ `missing_map` (an explicit
   integer key, e.g. `9: ".o"`) → that missing code.
5. **unmapped** — else → `missing_map.unmapped` (required if step 4 can fall
   through; otherwise a hard error).

6. **absent** (assembly, not per row) — an output unit the binding's TABLE has no row for (the
   table covers a subset of the roster: EU-SILC's personal file lists members aged 16+) →
   `missing_map.absent` when set; without it the cell stays NaN and the contract names it.

**Typed raw values (engine, topic 04).** Each binding reads ONE typed raw column — `numeric` or
`string`, from its storage. Map keys (`value_map`, `missing_map` specific keys) are typed to it:
integer codes on a numeric column; on a string column keys are QUOTED and matched verbatim
(`"01"` and `"1"` are different codes). A key of the other type is a spec error; a column mixing
numbers and strings, or a non-integer float in a `value_map` column, is a data error — nothing is
coerced or rounded.

**Unmapped is a finding (engine, topic 04).** A raw code that reaches step 5 FAILS the run (exit 1;
output and determinations still written) unless the binding waives it with a reason:

```yaml
missing_map:
  null: ".c"
  unmapped: {code: ".a", waive: "98/99 are don't-know/refused, expected in this item"}
```

The same rule applies to a `value_map_source` whose composition drops codes (a correspondence chain
that does not reach the level, a parameter row with no value): waive with `waive_dropped: <reason>`
on the `value_map_source`.

**Source sentinels (engine, topics 04 + 10).** A cell that carries NO value is a SOURCE sentinel,
kept apart from a plain null, whatever the delivery's encoding:

- a Stata extended missing (`.a`…`.z`) — `missing_map` may name it by its own string (`".a": ".b"`);
- an IN-BAND marker written into the column as a code (Survey Solutions `-999999999`, `##N/A##` on
  strings, a survey's `-99` / `9999`) — declared per column by the profile (the scan's negative
  labels, the source family's convention, the author's `sentinels`; an authored `value_codes` entry
  vetoes) and copied into `source_inventory.tables[].sentinels` at `--stamp`; `missing_map` may name
  it as a specific key (`"-999999999": ".c"`);
- a COMPANION FLAG code that means "no value" (EU-SILC `_F`: `-1` not filled, `-2` not applicable),
  declared in `tables[].flags[<col>].reasons` at `--stamp`; `missing_map` may name it as
  `"flag:-2": ".c"`.

An unnamed sentinel follows the `null` rule. A sentinel is never a value (a passthrough emits the
reason, not the marker), never "unmapped", and is counted per code in the determinations
(`sentinels`, `flags_seen`). Grounding never demands that a binding route a sentinel, and refuses a
`value_map` that maps one to a value. Any OTHER flag code qualifies a present value: a passthrough
binding carries it to the output (`<col>_flag`); a recode drops it, counted (`flag_dropped`). A
prelude sees raw markers as values — prelude code must treat the codes the card marks `sentinel` as
missing (NaN) itself.

`gate` grammar (a predicate whose **failing** rows get a code, distinct from
`predicate`, which defines the universe):

```yaml
gate:
  predicate: "age >= 6"     # weak grammar (§3.2); 6 = a mineducatage parameter (§4.1)
  else_code: ".c"
```

**Passthrough (identity emit).** A binding may set `passthrough: true` **instead
of** `value_map` (the two are mutually exclusive) to emit the `raw_value`
unchanged — an integer when whole, a float when continuous, a string otherwise.

finding on one is never put to the author: the flow leaves it out.

of `value_map`/`passthrough` — the three are mutually exclusive) to emit one
survey-level scalar at the grain: `countrycode: "GEO"`, `year: 2024`,
`mineducatage: 6`. No `raw_value` is needed; `table` names the roster so the value
lands on every output row. `gate` still applies (a scalar can be universe-bounded);
a whole-float emits as an int. `constant_source` REFERENCES the scalar instead of writing it:
`{parameter: PARAM-...}` (a scalar parameter: the spec's own `parameters` block for a survey
parameter, §4.1, else the country layer for `cvs_ref.country_layer`) or
`{survey_identity: iso3 | year}`; it is resolved into `constant` at run (the two are exclusive).
A gate predicate names a parameter by id the same way (`VAR-age >= PARAM-EDU-MIN-EDUCATION-AGE`,
§3.2) and the run substitutes the same value — never inline the threshold as a literal.

**Value-map source (country-parameter reference).** A binding may set
`value_map_source` **instead of** an inline `value_map` (the value modes —
`value_map` / `value_map_source` / `passthrough` / `constant` — are mutually
exclusive) to REFERENCE a governed country parameter instead of copying its map
into the spec. The recode map is resolved **at run time** from the country layer,
so the layer stays the single source of truth and a layer edit reaches the next
run with no spec regeneration. The canon it resolves from is the ONE version the
stamp names (`canon:` in the stamp, `spec/hspec.stamp.json`, from `gmd.cvs.canon_version()`): a
run on another installed version is refused by the gate and the flow re-validates
and re-stamps; `validate` resolves every reference on a copy first, so a parameter
with no record for the survey year, or a chain that drops codes without a
`waive_dropped`, is a finding in the authoring loop — nothing is persisted.

```yaml
value_map_source:
  parameter: PARAM-EDU-LEVEL-CROSSWALK   # a country-layer parameter id
  key: source_value                      # crosswalk row field matched to raw_value (raw code)
  value: gmd_educat7_code                # crosswalk row field emitted as the canonical code
```

(`{iso3, year}`), and lists the parameters it depends on in
`cvs_ref.country_parameters` (§1). The engine reads the country parameter for
that `iso3`+`year` (inclusive validity window, optional `selectors`), builds
`{row[key]: row[value]}` — coercing a boolean `improved_flag` to 0/1 and a
whole float to int — and applies it exactly like an inline `value_map` (so `gate`,
`missing_map`, `derived_from` all behave identically). A `mapping`-typed parameter
(a dict) is used directly. A referenced-but-unresolvable parameter is a hard error,
never a silent partial recode. The resolution is recorded as a determination (the
run-time audit trail). **All resolution happens product-side** in `gmd.hspec` through
the `gmd.cvs` API — the framework compiler reads no canon at all; it receives the
already-resolved `value_map` (and the contract records) from the product runner.

A `value_map_source` may instead reference the **layered correspondence** (the
survey → national standard → GMD chain in `gmd.cvs`, for education / water / sanitation /
geography) rather than a flat parameter. The survey's links are part of the spec: one
`correspondence` block per domain, written once for the survey column that carries the
domain's question, and read by every target of the domain.

```yaml
correspondence:
  education:
    column: q15                                  # the survey column whose codes are linked
    links:                                       # keyed by code, like a value_map
      "1": ARM-EDU-01                            # linked (the DEFAULT): a country_entry_id of the national standard
      "4": {kind: no_fitting_category, direct: {VAR-educat5: 4, VAR-educat4: 3},
            reason: "no national programme matches; the questionnaire defines it as post-secondary"}
      "6": {kind: ambiguous, candidates: [ARM-EDU-07, ARM-EDU-08],
            reason: "'college' is either vocational track; the questionnaire does not say which"}
      "9": {kind: residual, reason: "other (specify)"}
```

- The **column** is addressed as the tools print it: the bare name is required and sufficient when it is
  unique across the survey's tables; `table.column` is required when it is not, and is always accepted
  (it declares the binding's table).
- A **national category** (a `country_entry_id` of the country layer, in that domain, for the
  survey year `cvs_ref.country_layer.year`) is the default. The chain places it: national
  category → ISCED / JMP / GAUL → every target of the domain.
- Anything else is an **exception**, written `{kind, reason, …}` with one of the linking kinds
  (`harmon.records.reasons.LINK`) and the words that say why:
  - `no_fitting_category` — no national category means it. With `direct` it is placed: a value per
    target (the gated exception; a coarser level the author did not give follows from the canon
    recodes: educat7 → educat5 / educat4, educat5 → educat4, a fine WASH code → improved).
    Without `direct` it is not placed.
  - `ambiguous` — several categories fit and the survey cannot tell which: `candidates` lists them.
  - `residual` — other / don't know / refused: not a substantive answer.

  A code that is not placed lands on `.b` for every target of the domain; its reason is recorded.
- No labels: the survey's labels live in its profile; views join them by column + code.

  carry is an error, and so is a declared code the links neither link nor route.

rung or code (educat5 reads the educat5 slot, impwatrec the improved one, gauladm1code the GAUL
adm1 code):

```yaml

  target: VAR-educat5
  value_map_source: {correspondence: education}
  roles: {unit_keys: [uid, memberno]}            # raw_value OMITTED: read from the block's column
  missing_map: {unmapped: .b}                    #   (`validate --stamp` writes it, as it does `table`)
```

span straddles educat7's buckets, a direct edge that does not name it) is dropped from that
target's map — a sink, as for a flat parameter (waive it with `value_map_source.waive_dropped`).
A link to a category the country does not have is an error.

The chain is a **suggestion**. To deviate from it, keep the reference and record
per-code `overrides`, each with a mandatory `reason` — the base stays the reviewed
chain, only the named codes change, and every change is justified in the spec:

```yaml
value_map_source: {correspondence: education}
overrides:
  "7": {to: 7, reason: "national vocational → tertiary, not the ISCED upper-secondary the chain infers"}
```

domain, and on a retired `cvs_ref.instrument` pin. Under the product run path (`gmd hspec-run`)
this resolution — flat parameters and the correspondence chain alike — is performed
by `gmd.hspec` through the `gmd.cvs` API and handed to the framework compiler as a
concrete `value_map`; the framework never reads canon itself.


## 0. File format

The spec is ONE JSON file, a job's `spec/hspec.json` (UTF-8, written canonically by the tools: sorted
keys, 2-space indent). It is not hand-edited: bindings, headers, preludes and absences go in
through `gmd hspec-set-binding` / `hspec-set-header` / `hspec-set-prelude` /
`hspec-document-absent` (the host calls them with your JSON answers), and humans review it through
views, not as raw text.

- **Every map key is a string.** A `value_map` / `missing_map` code is written `"1"`, `"01"`,
  `"null"`; the engine types it from the raw column (an int code on a numeric column; the exact
  string on a string column, so `"01"` ≠ `"1"` there).
- **No comments.** Prose lives in fields: per-binding `evidence` / `note`, the `decision_log`, and
  the top-level `notes`.
- The examples below are annotated OUTLINES in a YAML-like notation for readability (`#` text is
  explanation, not content). The file itself is JSON, e.g. one binding:

```json
{"binding_id": "B-male", "kind": "recode", "target": "VAR-male", "table": "individuals",
 "roles": {"raw_value": "q1_sex", "unit_keys": ["uid", "memberno"]}, "predicate": "all",
 "value_map": {"1": 1, "2": 0}, "missing_map": {"null": ".c", "unmapped": ".a"},
 "register": "resolved", "evidence": "q1_sex labels 1=male 2=female (profile)"}
```

### 3.4 What `validate` checks, and what `--stamp` writes

`gmd validate` runs the ENGINE's own rules without data (`harmon.hspec.static`), with what the data
scan knows about each column: predicates and gate predicates parse, name columns of the binding's
frame and compare no numeric column with a string literal; map keys type to the raw column (two keys
that are one code — `"1"` and `"01"` on a numeric column — are an error); the `unmapped` waiver has
its reason; every code the binding can emit (map values, missing codes, `gate.else_code`,
`constant`, override `to`) is in the target's canon domain. Spec-wide: each target is bound once, a
name in `targets` has a binding, coverage statuses are from §5.

**Grounding (set equality).** A `value_map` on a raw column is checked against that column's domain
in its own table: what any channel declares (scan value labels, questionnaire categories, authored
codes) plus what the data holds. A key neither declared nor observed is an error (an invented code);
a declared code — or a value of a COMPLETE observed domain — that the binding does not handle
(`value_map` ∪ `missing_map` codes) is an error unless `missing_map.unmapped` is waived. By shape: a
one-hot member's domain is {0, 1} (plus what the scan declares, e.g. a sentinel); a linked
(by-reference) question is grounded by its observed domain. A column with no domain at all is a
warning (`severity: warning` in `--findings-json`).

**Blocked targets are excluded.** Validate checks the EFFECTIVE spec: a target with a `blocked`
coverage row (§5) is left out — its binding is neither checked nor run, nor is a prelude only blocked
targets read — so its findings no longer count; a block whose binding changed after the decision is
itself a finding (STALE: re-decide it). A produced binding that reads a blocked target
(`derived_from`, `gate_reads`) is a finding: block it too, or unblock the parent.

**Nothing waits for a person between the profile review and the output review (plan-12b).** The
read-only validate is the author's feedback loop: a finding the author has not seen goes back to it (an
automatic re-run); what is still open once the re-asks are used up is LEFT OUT by the flow — a `blocked`
row with `by: flow` and the kind of why (§5), every canon tier alike. A finding no target owns (the
header) cannot be left out: it is an error, and the run writes no output. Nobody signs the spec and
nobody approves a prelude before the run; a person reads the result at the output review (the spec's
open items, the registered `assumed` / `cannot_determine` judgments, the blocks and the documented
absences, beside the output and its measures) and may block a target (`gmd hspec-block <spec> --target
VAR-x --reason …`) or send it back to the author.

**The stamp.** `validate --stamp` refuses only a canon target of a declared module (`modules`) that is
neither bound, blocked nor documented — the authoring rule. Then it fills the mechanical coordinates — a binding's `table` and
`roles.unit_keys`, a table's `source_file` and `key_map` — marks each in `injected:` with where it
came from (`data_scan`, `overlay`, `prelude`, `parent`), re-validates the filled spec and stamps
only if that is clean. A table's keys come from, in order: the overlay's authored `tables[].keys`
verified unique (`profile/key_checks.json`, `--key-checks`), else the data scan's key when it is exact
(no duplicate rows — a capped candidate search does not matter once an exact key was found).
A scan key with duplicate rows is used when the scan EVIDENCED it (`pk_evidence`: another table's
key is contained in it — the scan's alias pass promotes such a near-unique column over an exact key
nothing joins on; the profile shows both candidates, `key.tolerant_joined`), and its duplicate rows
fall under rule 4 of §2.2. An unevidenced tolerant key, or no scan key, is never used silently —
the binding is a finding asking for an authored key. The stamp records what it was certified against: each input
file's sha256 and the profile bundle's `profile_sha`; and what was decided: the authored-content sha,
the blocked targets, and the COVERAGE TABLE — every canon variable
of the spec's modules with its module, tier and state (bound / blocked / documented with its status)
— with per-tier counts. The engine reports every target of that table in `targets.json` (§7).

## Definition
`gaul_adm1_code` is a numeric, country-specific variable that holds the Global
Administrative Unit Layers (GAUL) code for the first administrative level in
which the household is located. It is taken from the GAUL database (a copy is
available to the D4G team) where the geographic area can be identified in the
survey based on the location or area name.

## Conceptual intent
`gaul_adm1_code` provides a standardized, globally comparable code for the
first-level administrative division, independent of the survey's own classification.
It supports the cross-survey comparability of subnational statistics.

## Construction notes
`gaul_adm1_code` is numeric (integer) and country-specific, derived from the GAUL
database. The geographic area is identified in the survey on the basis of the
location or area name. The number of unique values from `subnatid1` and
`gaul_adm1_code` may be the same or different: e.g., if the survey is
representative at statistical regions while GAUL provides state-level codes, the
mapping reveals how the regions are constructed.
**Reusing the geography crosswalk.** Resolve `PARAM-GEO-GMD-CROSSWALK` from
the country layer for the survey ISO3 code and survey ID year (the same
match `VAR-geocode` performs). If the matched row has `geo_source: GAUL` and
a `geo_level` corresponding to the first administrative level, `geo_id` on
that row is already the GAUL code: set `gaul_adm1_code = int(geo_id)`
directly, with no separate GAUL database lookup required.
If the country's crosswalk instead uses a different `geo_source` (GADM,
NUTS, NSO, UN, DHS), the crosswalk does not carry a GAUL code for that
country; fall back to matching the household's recorded location name
directly against the GAUL database geometry as originally specified.
`value_codes` is intentionally null because GAUL codes come from an external
database (or, when available, the matched crosswalk row) and are not
enumerated in the harmonized value space.

## Consistency checks
- `gaul_adm1_code` must be numeric (integer).
- The code assigned must correspond to the GAUL first-level unit containing the
  household's recorded location.
- When sourced from the crosswalk, the matched row's `geo_source` must equal
  `GAUL`; never reinterpret a non-GAUL `geo_id` as a GAUL code.
- The number of distinct codes and their relationship to `subnatid1` must be
  documented and reviewed for plausibility.
- No household with an identifiable location may carry a standard missing (`.`).

## Escalation triggers
- The household's location cannot be matched to any GAUL first-level unit.
- The GAUL-to-survey mapping is internally inconsistent (e.g., one location maps
  to conflicting codes).
- The country's crosswalk uses a non-GAUL `geo_source` and no external GAUL
  database match is available either.

## Common mistakes
- Storing `gaul_adm1_code` as a string rather than an integer.
- Fabricating or renumbering GAUL codes instead of using the GAUL database
  (or the crosswalk's embedded GAUL `geo_id`).
- Confusing the GAUL first-level code with `subnatid1` values.
- Matching by name loosely and assigning the wrong GAUL unit.
- Treating `geo_id` from a non-GAUL-sourced crosswalk row as a genuine GAUL
  code.
